tier_reason: First-party README and docs/PERFORMANCE_NOTES.md numbers (M4 Mac, one synthetic 1.28 MB JSON file) with public benchmark scripts (benchmarks/benchmark-silesia.mjs, benchmark-brotli-minimal.mjs), but no rustc, Node or wasm-bindgen-lite version, the README does not say which script produced its rows, and the notes say gzip was built from a patched local flate2 1.1.7 that is not in the public Cargo.toml. The brotli level-11 row is invalid (mismatched work), so the claim is overstated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README/PERFORMANCE_NOTES on a 1.28 MB JSON file, M4 Mac: gzip vs pako level 1 ~3.8 vs ~14 ms (3.7x), level 6 ~7.0 vs ~22 ms (3.1x), level 9 ~11.7 vs ~58 ms (5.0x); lz4 vs lz4js ~1.4 vs ~4.0 ms (2.9x) and ~1.5 vs ~4.4 ms (2.9x) (the 'levels' are lz4js acceleration 1 and 9; the WASM lz4 has no levels); brotli quality 9 ~36 vs ~48.6 ms (1.35x) against the brotli npm package. The README's brotli 'level 11' row (~30 ms vs ~2.7 s, '90x') is invalid: bindings/brotli-wasm/wrapper.js maps every level above 6 to compress_level_9, so @addmaple/brotli ran quality 9 while the brotli npm package ran quality 11.
corrections.baseline: pako 2.1 (gzip, pure JS), lz4js 0.2 (pure JS LZ4 frame) and the brotli npm package 1.3.x (foliojs brotli.js, whose compressor is Google's C encoder compiled to JavaScript with Emscripten; not a native addon, although the README's Performance section calls it 'the native C implementation')
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust release profile opt-level = "z", lto = true (Cargo.toml); SIMD variant built with -C target-feature=+simd128, brotli SIMD variant on nightly with the portable_simd feature (scripts/build-all.sh); rustc, Node and wasm-bindgen-lite versions unstated (wasm-bindgen-lite devDependency is a local path, file:../wasm-bindgen-lite)
corrections.hardware: Apple M4 Mac (README; Node version unstated)
corrections.workload: Compressing one ~1.28 MB synthetic JSON file (likely test-data/silesia/large.json from benchmarks/gen_json.py, random records) in Node on an M4 Mac at several levels. The README does not name the script; benchmarks/benchmark-silesia.mjs (the npm run benchmark target) reports the mean of 3 timed runs after 2 warmups, while PERFORMANCE_NOTES labels its brotli table 'Median Time'.
corrections.caveats: The brotli level-11 '90x' row compares quality 9 (wrapper.js clamps levels above 6 to compress_level_9) against brotli.js at quality 11, so it is invalid; level 11 is not actually supported. The brotli baseline is an Emscripten-compiled C encoder running as JS, not native C. PERFORMANCE_NOTES says gzip used a patched local flate2 1.1.7, but the public Cargo.toml pins crates.io flate2 1.0 with zlib-rs, so the measured build may differ from the published code. The gzip path is a WASM build of zlib-rs (folded as a duplicate of zlib-ng) and the lz4 path a fork of lz4_flex (listed), so the entry is mostly packaging of listed codecs plus SIMD128 patches. Compressed sizes are not reported next to the times (zlib-rs level 1 uses a different strategy from pako level 1); the benchmark's compressionRatio helper is broken. One synthetic input, one machine, 3 runs; WASM is slower than the JS libraries below ~50 KB per the project's own notes.

notes: Real 3-5x gzip and ~2.9x lz4 wins over pure-JS pako and lz4js, first-party only; brotli wins only 1.35x at quality 9 against an Emscripten build. Record the level-11 90x row as invalid (level clamp in bindings/brotli-wasm/wrapper.js) and the possible wrapper relationship to zlib-rs/zlib-ng and lz4_flex. 3 stars, MIT, last commit 2026-01-19.

tier_reason: First-party README states only 'about 3x faster' than musescore -j, backed by the public script web-example/benchmark.js, with no published timings, hardware, MuseScore version or build flags; Boost Mode skips layout, so the two sides do unequal work.

corrections.baseline: The MuseScore 3 desktop binary's batch converter (spawn('musescore3', ['-j', batch.json]) exporting 200 .metajson files; installed version unstated), which is not told to skip layout
corrections.caveats: First-party; the README gives only 'about 3x' with no per-run numbers, hardware or MuseScore version. web-example/benchmark.js loads with doLayout=false (Boost Mode) and calls saveMetadata, while the native side runs a full musescore3 -j batch conversion, so the gap mostly measures skipped layout rather than WebAssembly beating native code. The native time is wall-clock around a spawned process with the first file's time subtracted via fs.watch as 'initialization'; the webmscore side excludes its own initialization. GPL-3.0-only with a font exception. Last commit 2023-01-24 on the webmscore branch.

notes: Claim matches the README ('about 3x faster than the batch converter feature (-j)'); numbers exist only as that ratio. The comparison is unequal work (layout skipped on the wasm side only); maintenance corrected from abandoned to stale (last commit 2023-01-24, under 3 years). License confirmed GPL-3.0-only from LICENSE.GPL; 182 stars, fork of musescore/MuseScore.

tier_reason: First-party README prose plus a table image (images/benchmark.png) of mean CPU and memory use during H.265 playback against three FFmpeg-based wasm players; no hardware, clip, browser, flags or benchmark code.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README (Chinese): on the developer's machine, for the same video, memory and CPU use differ little from the FFmpeg-based players of Taobao (Shoutao) and Huajiao, overall performance is about 5-10% better, and H.265 about 30% better because deblocking is reduced. The H.265 table image (images/benchmark.png) gives mean CPU / memory: WXInlinePlayer 64% / 162 MB, WASMVideoPlayer 102% / 197 MB, Taobao H265 91% / 174 MB, Huajiao H265 98% / 202 MB, i.e. about 30-37% less CPU (derived from page data).
corrections.baseline: FFmpeg-based wasm/asm.js H.264/H.265 web players: WASMVideoPlayer and the Taobao (Shoutao) and Huajiao implementations
corrections.license: Anti-996 License 1.0 (draft; non-OSI); package.json says ISC
corrections.workload: Playing the same FLV video (H.265 for the table) in a browser on the developer's machine and recording mean CPU and memory use; clip, resolution, browser and hardware unstated.
corrections.caveats: First-party prose and one screenshot table; no hardware, browser, clip or benchmark code. The H.265 gain is attributed to reduced deblocking, so the decoder likely does less filtering than a conforming FFmpeg HEVC decoder (output not shown to be equivalent). Two of the three baselines are closed commercial players. Anti-996 License (non-OSI, conflicting ISC in package.json), so reference only; bundles OpenH264, TinyH264 and libde265 decoders. Last commit 2022-03-26.

notes: The benchmark image is readable via raw.githubusercontent.com and contains the numbers the record lacked (CPU 64% vs 91-102%, memory 162 vs 174-202 MB); the record's 'memory and CPU about the same' paraphrase applies to the general comparison, not the H.265 table. Metric is CPU and memory, not throughput; the orchestrator may want to change the metric field. 1.5k stars, abandoned (last commit 2022-03-26).
